paper.title: Generative AI adoption in human creative tasks: Experimental evidence
paper.pdf_filename: Zhu and Zou (2026) - Generative AI Adoption in Human Creative Tasks.pdf
paper.version_read: Published journal version of record: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 242 (2026), 107414; DOI 10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107414. PDF p. 1: received 21 May 2025, revised 31 October 2025, accepted 1 January 2026, available online 15 January 2026.
paper.one_line_finding: Access to ChatGPT 3.5 raised the image-text creativity grade of students' picture ideas by 0.24 points on a 1-10 scale (0.32 SDs, SE 0.062, p < .01; control mean 5.93) relative to working alone (p. 7; Table 3 col 2, p. 8), while the text-only effect was 0.090 (SE 0.094) and not significant.
paper.shared_samples: Zhu and Zou (2023), 'The role of generative AI in human creative processes: experimental evidence', SSRN 4676053: the earlier working paper on the wave-1 participants, graded by two evaluators (p. 2, fn. 2; p. 22). The search record also lists SSRN 5196748 (2025) as a version of this paper; the document does not mention it. Holzner, Maier, and Feuerriegel (2025), a meta-analysis, includes this study (p. 3, fn. 3).

studies.label: Wave 1 lab experiment (HI vs HAT vs HHT), picture-idea tasks 2 and 3
studies.cluster_se_treatment: Robust standard errors are clustered by experimental session (PDF p. 8, Table 3; PDF p. 18, Appendix C). The session counts in clusters_per_arm are observed sessions from Table D.2, not proof of session randomization. Sessions contain participants and their repeated outputs, but individual versus session allocation and the random-effects grouping are not explicitly established. se_basis is unclear pending the allocation protocol; it is not coded output merely because the outcome rows are ideas.

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 2, Section 1; PDF p. 19, Table D.2 (columns Training, HAT, HI, HHT); exclusions in PDF p. 17, Appendix B.2
counts_source.quote: In the ﬁrst wave, 246 participants were recruited and randomly assigned to one of three between-subject treatments. ... No. subjects 56 61 63 122 No. sessions 2 2 2 5

arms.name: HI (Control)
arms.description: Human individual: treated picture-idea tasks alone without ChatGPT (PDF p. 4). All arms first received the same brief ChatGPT familiarization.

arms.name: HAT
arms.description: Human-AI team: individual participant may chat freely with ChatGPT 3.5 through Poe.com while producing picture ideas (PDF pp. 4, 6).

arms.name: HHT
arms.description: Human-human team: anonymous pairs, randomly re-matched for each treated task, converse by text and submit a shared idea (PDF p. 4).

studies.task: Nankai University students describe a creative picture in fewer than 100 Chinese characters within a 12-minute soft time limit for each of two counterbalanced themes; experimenters later generate images from the descriptions (PDF pp. 5-6).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT 3.5 accessed through poe.com
ai_tool.locator: PDF pp. 4, 6, Sections 2.1 and 2.3. First-wave deployment was May-June 2023; model release year is not stated. DALL-E 3 via ChatGPT-4o was used by experimenters to render outputs, not supplied to participants (PDF p. 17).

preregistration.where: AsPredicted.org; PDF p. 6, Section 2.3. Registration and deviations are in Supplementary Section 1, not on file.

studies.shared_sample: Earlier working paper Zhu and Zou (2023), The role of generative AI in human creative processes: experimental evidence, SSRN 4676053, used the same first-wave participants with an earlier evaluation panel (PDF p. 2, footnote 2; PDF p. 22). The citation record also identifies SSRN 5196748 as a version; its overlap is not separately established in this PDF.

estimates.outcome: Image-text creativity grade, pooled themes; Table 3 column 1 without participant covariates
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Mean creativity grade from 30 student evaluators per theme, using a 1-10 scale to one decimal place. Evaluators saw the submitted description and its experimenter-generated DALL-E 3 image. Theme order and evaluation-format order were counterbalanced. Image-text grades are the paper’s primary measure, but preregistered-primary status is unverified.

regression.model: Random-effects grade model with treatment indicators, theme and task-order indicators; no participant covariates. Outcome rows are individual/team ideas. Robust SEs are clustered by session; the random-effects grouping is not specified.

sources.quote: Random-eﬀect models with robust standard errors clustered at the session level (reported in parentheses).

estimates.notes: The retained model has no participant covariates. Models using major, collected in final Questionnaire III, are excluded under extraction rule 5 (PDF pp. 8, 16). Table 2 supplies descriptive raw arm means and SDs; the SD aggregation is unresolved, so sd_level remains null. n_units is the printed observation count for the entire model, including the other first-wave arm and the nonrandom Training cohort, not the number of people or the count for this pairwise contrast. Submission counts are not converted to people. The allocation unit and random-effects grouping are unresolved: the printed session clustering is retained, but se_basis is unclear and the uncertainty is not eligible for pooling. This is a between-arm comparison; repeated themes do not make it a paired or first-round contrast. The paper names image-text grades as its primary outcome; this is the eligible pooled-theme specification without participant covariates. The rounded adjusted effect and its standardized counterpart in Section 3.2 are excluded, not attached to this specification.
estimates.primary_override_reason: Rule 2: All candidates share the paper's primary image-text outcome, but its main analysis pools both treated tasks on the raw grade scale; within-evaluator standardization and separate-theme analyses are described as robustness variants. The adjusted estimate highlighted in the introduction is excluded in the source extraction, leaving Table 3 column (1) as the eligible pooled raw-grade regression. (PDF p. 2, Section 1, final paragraph; pp. 7-8, Section 3.2, Table 3 column (1) and the final robustness paragraph on p. 8.: "Our results show that access to ChatGPT in the HAT treatment improves creative performance by 0.24 points (0.32 SDs, 𝑝< .01) compared to the HI treatment, whose mean grade is 5.93 points.")

estimates.question: with_ai

estimates.outcome: Coefficient of variation of creativity grades, Here
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Treatment-by-theme performance inequality derived from human creativity grades. CV is SD divided by mean grade; Gini concerns potential payments under a rule linear in the grade without a fixed component (PDF p. 10, Table 5). Underlying grade format and aggregation level are not identified.

Mean fields store published arm-level indices, not participant means. No uncertainty, exact analysis counts or pairwise differences are reported.

not_extracted.what: S2: all Training-cohort outcomes S2-O1 through S2-O7, including Training versus HI, HAT, or HHT
not_extracted.reason: Nonrandom comparison with separately recruited first-wave arms. Sections 1 and 2.1 (PDF pp. 3, 5) explicitly discuss time-lag and sample-selection limitations; the generic random-distribution statement in Appendix B.2 does not resolve the contradiction.

not_extracted.what: S3: Standalone ChatGPT versus human or human-AI outputs (PDF p. 12; Tables D.4-D.5, PDF p. 20)
not_extracted.reason: The AI-only arm contains no person receiving assistance. Human-arm descriptive cells are retained separately without importing model-only comparison tests.

not_extracted.what: Hypothetical human-AI and human-human team benchmarks (PDF p. 12, Section 4.1)
not_extracted.reason: Simulated pairings and mechanically selected maxima are not randomized groups of people who worked in those conditions.

not_extracted.what: S1-O4: Post-treatment original DAT score
not_extracted.reason: Output-scored original DAT measures within-person flexibility, but AI availability during the post-task test is unstated (PDF pp. 4, 16-17), so with_ai versus after_ai cannot be confirmed. Figure 4b has no numerical coefficient or interval endpoints (PDF p. 11); PDF p. 12 reports a nonsignificant effect. Its model also adjusts for unbalanced controls, including major collected in final Questionnaire III (PDF pp. 8, 11, 16, 18), and is excluded under rule 5. No figure values are estimated.

not_extracted.what: S1-O5: Post-treatment modified-DAT score
not_extracted.reason: Output-scored modified DAT measures novelty relative to supplied words (PDF pp. 16-17). AI availability during the post-task test is unstated, preventing with_ai/after_ai classification. PDF p. 12, Section 3.4, prints: experiencing ChatGPT access and experiencing teamwork both lead to an increase of 0.19 SDs in the modiﬁed-DAT score; The Figure 4b model also adjusts for unbalanced controls, including major collected in final Questionnaire III (PDF pp. 8, 11, 16, 18), and is excluded under rule 5. Exact raw coefficients, SEs and analyzed-person counts are absent; no figure values are estimated.

open_items: Individual versus session allocation and the random-effects grouping remain unestablished. Table D.2 session counts are observed clusters, not proof of session randomization. Session clustering encompasses repeated outputs within sessions; resolving the allocation protocol is necessary for definitive participant versus randomized-cluster se_basis. Retained model uncertainty is coded unclear (PDF pp. 2, 6, 8, 18-19).

Exact analyzed-person counts by arm and outcome are not printed. The recruitment counts and Appendix B.2 exclusions are insufficient under the transcribe-only rule: do not subtract exclusions, divide submission counts, sum arm counts, or relabel regression rows as people (PDF pp. 4, 8, 17, 19).

Identify the level of Table 2 SDs: participant means, output means, individual ratings or another aggregation. Its averaging language does not establish an unambiguous usable participant SD; sd_level remains null (PDF pp. 7-8, 18).

Confirm AI availability during original and modified post-task DAT and obtain eligible coefficients without adjustment for variables measured after treatment. Exact raw coefficients, uncertainty and analyzed-person counts are absent (PDF pp. 4, 11-12, 16-18).

Specify which grade format and observations underlie Table 5 CV and Gini, together with analysis counts and uncertainty. These indices measure performance inequality, not diversity of content (PDF p. 10).

Separate supplementary preregistration, deviations, allocation instructions, DAT instructions and Tables S1-S7 remain unavailable. Preregistered-primary status cannot be confirmed from the published-paper primary label (PDF pp. 6, 8, 21).
ChatGPT 3.5 model release year is not stated; experimental deployment dates are not used as a release year (PDF pp. 4, 6).

No eligible numerical direct HAT-versus-HHT uncertainty is established for the retained descriptive summaries. Stars in Tables D.4-D.5 compare each arm with standalone ChatGPT and cannot be used for contrasts between human arms (PDF pp. 7, 20).

review_corrections.basis: PDF p. 19, Table D.2 lists the sessions by treatment (HAT 2, HI 2, HHT 5), so every session ran one arm and its participants shared their arm; under the codebook section 3, session rule (added during Phase 2, 2026-10-10, for review) the assignment unit is the session. Table 3 clusters its robust SEs by session (PDF p. 8, notes).

Table 3's SEs are clustered by session, and the session is the assignment unit under the codebook section 3, session rule (added during Phase 2, 2026-10-10, for review). The record was unclear only because the allocation unit was open.
